80443055.title: Red and Purple Modernization Project
80443055.extract:
The Red and Purple Modernization (RPM) Project is a multi-phased reconstruction project coordinated by the Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) in the North Side of Chicago, Evanston, and Wilmette. As part of the broader Red Ahead program, the RPM project plans to replace aging infrastructure on the North Side main line north of Belmont station and the Evanston branch. The latter branch is served by the Purple Line, while the former north of Belmont station is served by the Red Line and the Purple Line Express. Both of the Chicago "L" branches were built between 1900 and 1912, with most of the section north of Wilson station being embanked by 1931.
Early planning for the project began in 2009 with a vision study, which assessed the conditions of the two branches. The CTA opted for modernization in 2011. Construction for Phase One of the project occurred from October 2, 2019, to July 20, 2025. At the junction between the North Side main line and the Ravenswood branch (Clark Junction), the Red-Purple Bypass Project replaced a level junction with a flying junction, allowing northbound Brown Line trains to cross above main line tracks. Additionally, Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr stations as well as a section of the viaduct hosting these stations were rebuilt.


== Background ==
On May 31, 1900, the Northwestern Elevated Railroad Company opened the North Side main line from the Loop Elevated to Wilson station. In 1907, the Ravenswood branch opened from the newly built Clark Junction north of Belmont station to Kimball station. In 1908, the main line was extended along an existing at-grade railroad, which was built by the Chicago and Evanston Railroad (C&E), to Central station in Evanston. In 1912, the line was extended to Linden station in Wilmette.
From 1908 to 1931, the North Side main line and the Evanston branch were being elevated piecemeal from Wilson to Isabella stations. An embankment was chosen to safely convey heavy C&E freight trains, which ran along the embanked "L" tracks until April 30, 1973. Embankment tracks remained in use for rapid transit service.


== Early planning ==

Between 2009 and 2010, the CTA conducted a vision study surrounding the North Side main line and the Evanston branch from Belmont to Linden stations. Deteriorating track conditions and old railroad signals have contributed to slow zones on both branches. In addition, many stations on the said branches were not compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) due to a lack of accessibility features, and existing station capacity was not enough to accommodate growing ridership. In October 2010, the CTA chose modernization as the locally preferred alternative.
In January 2011, the CTA and the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) began drafting the environmental impact statement (EIS) for the "Red and Purple Modernization Project". From that same month, public meetings on the project were held. During the planning process, several alternatives that were once considered were dropped, such as a new elevated viaduct with one fewer track and a double-track subway line.
In November 2013, the CTA applied for the Core Capacity grant from the FTA. The transit agency initially received $35 million in August 2014.
Earlier in 2014, the CTA made the decision to divide the RPM project into phases. A new EIS was being drafted for just Phase One (Red-Purple Bypass at Clark Junction and the Lawrence–Bryn Mawr segment), which concluded in 2015 with two Categorical Exclusions and two Findings of No Significant Impact.
On November 30, 2016, the Chicago City Council implemented a 36-year tax increment financing (TIF) district around much of the North Side main line for the modernization project. The potential revenue from TIF allowed the CTA to obtain a total of $1.1 billion in federal funding, which was finalized in January 2017 under a Full Funding Grant Agreement with the FTA. Federal funding included $956.61 million in Core Capacity grant and $115.73 million in Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality grant; local funding included $610.06 million from TIF revenue and $384.30 million from CTA sales tax revenue. The overall project cost for Phase One was set to $2.1 billion.
In June 2017, the CTA filed a Request for Qualifications in search of a project contractor. On December 13, 2018, through a $1.2 billion contract, the CTA selected Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team (Walsh Group and Fluor Corporation) as the general contractor for RPM Phase One.


=== Interim improvements ===
In 2012, a segment of the North Side main line between Wilson and Jarvis was rehabilitated as part of the $86-million Red North Station Interim Improvements project. Kiewit Infrastructure, the project contractor, received $57.4 million. Multiple stations except for Wilson, Bryn Mawr, and Loyola were temporarily closed and renovated in six-week phases from June to December 2012. In June 2013, the CTA announced the installation of public artworks in all of the rehabilitated stations.
In a separate project between 2012 and 2013, Loyola station received a $17 million renovation that included the addition of an adjacent public plaza. Kiewit Infrastructure was also the contractor for the renovation.
Before the mid-2010s, Wilson station had an unusual track configuration where the southbound express track briefly shifted away from the main line. The shift was designed to connect the North Side main line with the now-demolished C&E tracks. Between 2014 and 2017, the station was entirely reconstructed as part of a $203 million project, which added Purple Line Express service on the station.


=== Criticism ===
The CTA had originally considered consolidating closely spaced stations to reduce train travel times. This proposal was eventually dropped as nearby residents and aldermen criticized it as a form of service cuts.
Residents near Clark Junction criticized the Brown Line flyover, citing the demolition of 16 homes and the flyover being visually imposing. Then-mayoral candidate Chuy García also criticized the flyover as "an unnecessary expenditure of taxpayer funds that will generate little return on investment".


== Phase One construction ==
Phase One construction began with a groundbreaking ceremony on October 2, 2019. Construction took place around Clark Junction and a section between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr stations.


=== Lawrence to Bryn Mawr ===

The project was divided into two stages, each of which involved temporarily rerouting trains onto a pair of tracks. The CTA constructed interlockings near Montrose and Thorndale avenues in preparation for stage A. The CTA also constructed temporary station facilities for Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations; Lawrence and Berwyn stations were anticipated to be closed throughout two stages of construction. Due to a physically constrained construction area, the new viaduct was constructed out of precast segmental box girders using a launching gantry.
Stage A began on May 16, 2021, with the closure of Lawrence and Berwyn stations and the opening of temporary station facilities at Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations. Trains were rerouted onto the two westernmost tracks to make way for the replacement of the two easternmost tracks.
Stage A construction concluded on July 28, 2023, with the beginning of Stage B. Trains were rerouted onto two newly rebuilt tracks while construction began on the two westernmost tracks. Argyle station was relocated to Foster Avenue and Winona Street; Bryn Mawr station became only accessible to or from 95th-bound Red Line trains. Construction on permanent station facilities at Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr stations began.
These permanent facilities opened on July 20, 2025.


==== Public space ====
The replacement of embankment tracks opened up ten blocks of public space below the rail line. In 2024, during construction, the CTA held a series of public meetings on the new public space and its potential amenities. The design for the space was finalized in February 2025 with the addition of a footpath, parking spaces, and recreational amenities. Construction on the space is slated to occur from 2026 to 2027.


=== Red-Purple Bypass ===

Before the project, Clark Junction was a level junction, which required northbound Brown Line trains to cross main line tracks at grade.
The Red-Purple Bypass Project called for a 45-foot-high (14 m) Brown Line flyover ramp as well as a straighter alignment on the main line north of Belmont. The flyover was constructed out of steel plate girders, while the new main line viaduct was largely constructed out of precast prestressed concrete girders. With the exception of the straddle bent, which spans above the main line, the concrete piers for the flyover have decorative groove marks.
Construction began in 2019 with the installation of a flyover ramp. The flyover opened to Brown Line service on the early morning of November 19, 2021. On March 3, 2022, inspectors reported concrete spalling on the flyover walls as a result of frost weathering. Although the structural integrity of the flyover remained intact, these damages were fully repaired in December 2022.
In August 2021, the Vautravers Building was moved westward to make way for straightening the main line north of Belmont. Construction on the new alignment began in late 2021. The two westernmost tracks were first rebuilt, which reopened to service in December 2023. The two easternmost tracks were then closed for reconstruction until 2025.


== Future phases ==
The CTA is currently studying the rest of the phases surrounding the Evanston branch and the remaining segments of the North Side main line from Addison to Sheridan and from Thorndale to Howard. The RPM Next Phases Study was conducted from 2021 to 2024. Several public meetings were held: two in March 2023, one in November 2023, and one in February 2024.
The project timeline is currently undetermined due to a lack of federal funding. In October 2025, at the start of the 2025 United States federal government shutdown, Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought withheld a combined $2.1 billion for the Red Line Extension and the Red and Purple Modernization Project, citing reports of diversity, equity, and inclusion practices that he described as "unconstitutional". 


== See also ==
Brown Line Capacity Expansion Project – reconstruction project on the Brown Line in the 2000s
Red Line Extension – large-scale project on the Red Line as part of the Red Ahead program

== General references ==

The '''Red and Purple Modernization''' ('''RPM''') '''Project''' is a multi-phased reconstruction project coordinated by the [[Chicago Transit Authority]] (CTA) in the [[North Side, Chicago|North Side]] of [[Chicago]], [[Evanston, Illinois|Evanston]], and [[Wilmette, Illinois|Wilmette]]. As part of the broader [[Red Ahead]] program, the RPM project plans to replace aging infrastructure on the [[North Side main line]] north of [[Belmont station (CTA North Side Main Line)|Belmont station]] and the [[Evanston branch]]. The latter branch is served by the [[Purple Line (CTA)|Purple Line]], while the former north of Belmont station is served by the [[Red Line (CTA)|Red Line]] and the Purple Line Express. Both of the [[Chicago "L"]] branches were built between 1900 and 1912, with most of the section north of [[Wilson station (CTA)|Wilson station]] being embanked by 1931.

Early planning for the project began in 2009 with a vision study<!--the '''North Red and Purple Line Vision Study'''-->, which assessed the conditions of the two branches. The CTA opted for modernization in 2011. Construction for Phase One of the project occurred from October 2, 2019, to July 20, 2025. At the junction between the North Side main line and the [[Ravenswood branch]] (Clark Junction), the '''Red-Purple Bypass Project''' replaced a [[level junction]] with a [[flying junction]], allowing northbound Brown Line trains to cross above main line tracks. Additionally, {{cta|Lawrence}}, {{cta|Argyle}}, {{cta|Berwyn}}, and {{cta|Bryn Mawr}} stations as well as a section of the viaduct hosting these stations were rebuilt.

==Background==
On May 31, 1900, the [[Northwestern Elevated Railroad|Northwestern Elevated Railroad Company]] opened the North Side main line from the [[Loop Elevated]] to Wilson station.<ref name="EdgewaterHist">{{cite web |title=Edgewater's Second Railroad |url=https://www.edgewaterhistory.org/ehs/local/edgewaters-second-railroad |website=Edgewater Historical Society |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref><ref name=Tribune19000531>{{cite news |title=New "L" Road is Opened |newspaper=Chicago Daily Tribune |date=June 1, 1900 |page=2}}</ref> In 1907, the [[Ravenswood branch]] opened from the newly built Clark Junction north of Belmont station to [[Kimball station]].<ref name="Ravenswood open">{{cite news |title=New 'L' Line Operated |newspaper=Chicago Daily Tribune |date=May 19, 1907 |page=11}}</ref>{{sfn|Borzo|2007|p=133}} In 1908, the main line was extended along an existing at-grade railroad, which was built by the [[Chicago and Evanston Railroad]] (C&E), to [[Central station (CTA Purple Line)|Central station]] in Evanston. In 1912, the line was extended to [[Linden station (CTA)|Linden station]] in Wilmette.<ref name="EdgewaterHist"/><ref name="SRJ1908">{{cite journal|title=The Northwestern Elevated Extension at Evanston, ILL|journal=The Street Railway Journal|date=May 23, 1908|volume=31|issue=21|pages=842–849|url=https://libraryarchives.metro.net/DPGTL/ERJ/srj-street-railway-journal/1908-srj-volume-31-no-21-may-23.pdf}}</ref>{{sfn|Borzo|2007|p=80–81}}

From 1908 to 1931, the North Side main line and the Evanston branch were being elevated piecemeal from Wilson to {{cta|Isabella}} stations.<ref name="Howard branch">{{cite web |last=Garfield |first=Graham |title=North Side Main Line (Howard branch) |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/operations/lines/northmain-red.html |website=Chicago-L.org |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Garfield |first=Graham |title=Evanston |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/operations/lines/evanston.html |website=Chicago-L.org |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref> An [[embankment (earthworks)|embankment]] was chosen to safely convey heavy C&E freight trains, which ran along the embanked "L" tracks until April 30, 1973. Embankment tracks remained in use for rapid transit service.<ref name="freightL">{{cite web |last=Garfield |first=Graham |title=Freight Service on the "L" |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/operations/freight/index.html |website=Chicago-L.org |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref>{{sfn|Borzo|2007|p=70}}<ref name="embankment">{{cite web |title=Why is our L on an embankment |url=https://www.edgewaterhistory.org/ehs/local/why-is-our-L-on-an-embankment |website=Edgewater Historical Society }}</ref>

In January 2011, the CTA and the [[Federal Transit Administration]] (FTA) began drafting the [[environmental impact statement]] (EIS) for the "Red and Purple Modernization Project". From that same month, public meetings on the project were held.<ref name="Howard branch"/><ref>{{cite serial |credits= |title=WGN News at Nine |last= |first= |episode= |date=27 January 2011 |episode-link= |url=https://archive.org/details/WGN_20110128_030000_WGN_News_at_Nine/start/754/end/921 |archive-url= |archive-date=<!--18 April 2011-->|location=Chicago, Illinois |series= |series-link= |language=en |publisher= |time=9:12 pm–9:15 pm CST |network= |station=[[WGN-TV]] |access-date= |quote= |trans-quote=}}</ref> During the planning process, several alternatives that were once considered were dropped, such as a new elevated viaduct with one fewer track and a double-track subway line.<ref name="Howard branch"/>

In November 2013, the CTA applied for the Core Capacity grant from the FTA.<ref name="DOT 2020"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hilkevitch |first1=Jon |title=Plan to rebuild Red, Purple Lines gets boost from federal government |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2013/11/19/plan-to-rebuild-red-purple-lines-gets-boost-from-federal-government/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=19 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131211075912/http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/local/breaking/chi-plan-to-rebuild-red-purples-lines-gets-boost-from-federal-government-20131119,0,7074567.story |archive-date=11 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Smith |first=Stephen J. |title=Chicago Becomes First City to Apply for FTA's Capacity-Boosting Transit Grants |url=https://nextcity.org/urbanist-news/chicago-first-city-apply-fta-capacity-boosting-transit-grants |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=[[Next City]] |date=20 November 2013}}</ref> The transit agency initially received $35 million in August 2014.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Laing |first1=Keith |title=Feds award Chicago subway $35M grant |url=https://thehill.com/policy/transportation/214644-feds-award-chicago-subway-35m-grant/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=[[The Hill (newspaper)|The Hill]] |date=7 August 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Nunez |first1=Jenifer |title=CTA awarded federal Core Capacity funds for red, purple line modernization |url=https://www.rtands.com/passenger/rapid-transit-light-rail/cta-awarded-federal-core-capacity-funds-for-red-purple-line-modernization/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=Railway Track and Structures |date=8 August 2014}}</ref>

Earlier in 2014, the CTA made the decision to divide the RPM project into phases.<ref name="DOT 2020"/> A new EIS was being drafted for just Phase One (Red-Purple Bypass at Clark Junction and the Lawrence–Bryn Mawr segment),<ref name="Howard branch"/> which concluded in 2015 with two Categorical Exclusions and two Findings of No Significant Impact.<ref name="DOT 2020"/>

On November 30, 2016, the [[Chicago City Council]] implemented a 36-year tax increment financing (TIF) district around much of the North Side main line for the modernization project. The potential revenue from TIF allowed the CTA to obtain a total of $1.1 billion in federal funding,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Griffin-Stegink |first1=Ryan |title=City Council Approves TIF for Transit |url=https://metroplanning.org/city-council-approves-tif-for-transit/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Metropolitan Planning Council |date=1 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Red-Purple Modernization (RPM) Phase One Project TIF |url=https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/dcd/supp_info/tif/red-and-purple-modernization-phase-one-project-tif.html |website=City of Chicago |access-date=16 July 2025}}</ref> which was finalized in January 2017 under a Full Funding Grant Agreement with the FTA. Federal funding included $956.61 million in Core Capacity grant and $115.73 million in Congestion Mitigation and Air Quality grant; local funding included $610.06 million from TIF revenue and $384.30 million from CTA sales tax revenue. The overall project cost for Phase One was set to $2.1 billion.<ref name="Howard branch"/><ref name="DOT 2020"/>

In June 2017, the CTA filed a Request for Qualifications in search of a project contractor.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Koziarz |first1=Jay |title=CTA moves forward with ambitious Red/Purple Line plan |url=https://chicago.curbed.com/2017/6/9/15771036/chicago-transporation-cta-red-purple-line-belmont-flyover |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Curbed Chicago |date=9 June 2017 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Koziarz |first1=Jay |title=The CTA reveals short list of three firms to build Red, Purple Line modernization project |url=https://chicago.curbed.com/2017/12/8/16751420/transportation-cta-belmont-flyover-construction |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Curbed Chicago |date=8 December 2017 |language=en}}</ref> On December 13, 2018, through a $1.2 billion contract, the CTA selected Walsh-Fluor Design Build Team (Walsh Group and Fluor Corporation) as the general contractor for RPM Phase One.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wanek-Libman |first1=Mischa |title=CTA approves two contracts to advance Red Line improvement projects |url=https://www.masstransitmag.com/rail/infrastructure/article/21036780/cta-approves-two-contracts-to-advance-red-line-improvement-projects |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Mass Transit Magazine |date=13 December 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wronski |first1=Richard |title=CTA awards contract for $1.2 billion Red Line project |url=https://www.trains.com/trn/news-reviews/news-wire/14-cta-awards-contract-for-12-billion-red-line-project/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Trains Magazine |date=15 December 2018}}</ref>

===Interim improvements===
In 2012, a segment of the North Side main line between Wilson and {{cta|Jarvis}} was rehabilitated as part of the $86-million '''Red North Station Interim Improvements''' project. [[Kiewit Corporation|Kiewit Infrastructure]], the project contractor, received $57.4 million.<ref name="CBS 2012">{{cite news |title=CTA To Begin Overhaul Of 7 Aging Red Line Stations |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/cta-to-begin-overhaul-of-7-aging-red-line-stations/ |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=CBS Chicago |date=27 April 2012}}</ref> Multiple stations except for {{cta|Wilson}}, {{cta|Bryn Mawr}}, and {{cta|Loyola}} were temporarily closed and renovated in six-week phases from June to December 2012.<ref name="Howard branch"/><ref>{{cite news |last1=Woodard |first1=Benjamin |title=Jarvis Red Line Station Construction Worries Local Business Owners |url=https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20121102/rogers-park/jarvis-red-line-station-construction-worries-local-business-owners/ |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=DNAinfo Chicago |date=2 November 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107192701/https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20121102/rogers-park/jarvis-red-line-station-construction-worries-local-business-owners |archive-date=7 November 2017 }}</ref> In June 2013, the CTA announced the installation of public artworks in all of the rehabilitated stations.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Spula |first1=Ian |title=CTA Releases Images of Winning Red Line Station Art Work |url=https://chicago.curbed.com/2013/6/18/10231452/cta-renders-selection-of-art-for-rehabbed-red-line-stations |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=Curbed Chicago |date=18 June 2013 |language=en}}</ref>

In a separate project between 2012 and 2013, Loyola station received a $17 million renovation that included the addition of an adjacent public plaza. Kiewit Infrastructure was also the contractor for the renovation.<ref>{{cite web |title=CTA Station and Plaza Updates |url=https://www.luc.edu/communityrelations/currentprojects/ctastationandplazaupdates/ |website=Loyola University Chicago |access-date=15 July 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Woodard |first1=Benjamin |title=Pols Unveil $17 Million Renovation of Loyola 'L' Station |url=https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20131108/rogers-park/pols-unveil-17-million-renovation-of-loyola-l-station/slideshow/459087/ |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=DNAinfo Chicago |date=8 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171113200904/https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20131108/rogers-park/pols-unveil-17-million-renovation-of-loyola-l-station/slideshow/459087/ |archive-date=13 November 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Garfield |first=Graham |title=Loyola |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/stations/loyola.html |website=Chicago-L.org |access-date=15 July 2025}}</ref>

Before the mid-2010s, Wilson station had an unusual track configuration where the southbound express track briefly shifted away from the main line. The shift was designed to connect the North Side main line with the now-demolished C&E tracks.<ref name="freightL"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Rapid Transit Map |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/maps/track/1965dec_N-S2.pdf |publisher=Chicago Transit Authority |date=December 1965 |access-date=17 December 2023}}</ref> Between 2014 and 2017, the station was entirely reconstructed as part of a $203 million project, which added Purple Line Express service on the station.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kamin |first1=Blair |title=New Wilson station shows CTA’s Red-Purple Line modernization is on track |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2017/11/10/new-wilson-station-shows-ctas-red-purple-line-modernization-is-on-track/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=10 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Senese |first1=Kyra |title=CTA completes Wilson Station reconstruction project |url=https://www.rtands.com/passenger/commuter-regional/cta-completes-wilson-station-reconstruction-project/ |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=Railway Track and Structures |date=7 February 2018}}</ref>

===Criticism===
The CTA had originally considered consolidating closely spaced stations to reduce train travel times. This proposal was eventually dropped as nearby residents and aldermen criticized it as a form of service cuts.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hilkevitch |first1=Jon |title=CTA puts brakes on talk of closing Red Line stations |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2011/01/30/cta-puts-brakes-on-talk-of-closing-red-line-stations/ |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=30 January 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130606110814/https://articles.chicagotribune.com/2011-01-30/classified/ct-met-getting-around-0131-20110130_1_station-closings-red-line-cta-vice-president |archive-date=6 June 2013}}</ref>

Residents near Clark Junction criticized the Brown Line flyover, citing the demolition of 16 homes and the flyover being visually imposing. Then-mayoral candidate [[Chuy García]] also criticized the flyover as "an unnecessary expenditure of taxpayer funds that will generate little return on investment".<ref>{{multiref2
|{{cite news |last1=Rossi |first1=Rosalind |title=Garcia criticizes Ashland bus rapid transit plan; Claypool insists it’s ‘not a done deal’ |url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/3/11/18483680/garcia-criticizes-ashland-bus-rapid-transit-plan-claypool-insists-it-s-not-a-done-deal |access-date=29 July 2025 |work=Chicago Sun-Times |date=12 March 2015 |language=en }}
|{{cite news |last1=Swartz |first1=Tracy |title=Chicago mayoral candidates sound off on transit priorities |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2015/03/02/chicago-mayoral-candidates-sound-off-on-transit-priorities/ |access-date=29 July 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=2 March 2015 }}
|{{cite news |last1=Greenfield |first1=John |title=Checkerboard City: Transit Platforms |url=https://www.newcity.com/2015/03/30/checkerboard-city-transit-platforms/ |access-date=29 July 2025 |work=New City |date=30 March 2015}}
}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Woodard |first1=Benjamin |last2=Dai |first2=Serena |title=CTA's Belmont Bypass: 16 Existing Buildings Needed for New Flyover |url=https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20140417/lakeview/ctas-belmont-station-bypass-16-lakeview-buildings-needed |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=DNAinfo Chicago |date=17 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107193633/https://www.dnainfo.com/chicago/20140417/lakeview/ctas-belmont-station-bypass-16-lakeview-buildings-needed |archive-date=7 November 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Hinz |first1=Greg |title=CTA moves to unsnarl North Side el tracks |url=https://www.chicagobusiness.com/article/20140417/BLOGS02/140419787/cta-moves-to-unsnarl-north-side-snafus-for-red-brown-purple-lines |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Crain's Chicago Business |date=17 April 2014}}</ref>

==Phase One construction==
Phase One construction began with a groundbreaking ceremony on October 2, 2019. Construction took place around Clark Junction and a section between Lawrence and Bryn Mawr stations.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Freund |first1=Sara |title=Work begins on Red-Purple Line project replacing 119-year-old rails, worn stations |url=https://chicago.curbed.com/2019/10/2/20895832/cta-construction-red-purple-project-begins |access-date=15 July 2025 |work=Curbed Chicago |date=2 October 2019 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wanek-Libman |first1=Mischa |title=CTA begins Phase One of $2.1-billion Red and Purple Modernization Project |url=https://www.masstransitmag.com/rail/infrastructure/article/21108807/cta-begins-phase-one-of-21-billion-red-and-purple-modernization-project |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=Mass Transit Magazine |date=3 October 2019 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Briginshaw |first1=David |title=Chicago breaks ground on Red and Purple line modernisation project |url=https://www.railjournal.com/infrastructure/chicago-breaks-ground-on-red-and-purple-line-modernisation-project/ |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=International Railway Journal |date=3 October 2019}}</ref>

===Lawrence to Bryn Mawr===
[[File:Bryn Mawr temporary southbound station stairs to platform, December 2020 (50758909363).jpg|thumb|alt=Construction on the temporary station facility at Bryn Mawr station in December 2020|Temporary station facility at [[Bryn Mawr station (CTA)|Bryn Mawr station]], December 2020]]
[[File:Bryn Mawr station Stage B (July 2023).jpg|thumb|alt=Temporary platform at Bryn Mawr station in July 2023 after trains were relocated to the newer tracks|Bryn Mawr station platform during Stage B construction, July 2023]]

The project was divided into two stages, each of which involved temporarily rerouting trains onto a pair of tracks. The CTA constructed interlockings near Montrose and Thorndale avenues in preparation for stage A. The CTA also constructed temporary station facilities for Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations; Lawrence and Berwyn stations were anticipated to be closed throughout two stages of construction.<ref>{{cite news |title=CTA to Close 2 North Side Stations During First Phase of Modernization Project |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/cta-to-close-2-north-side-stations-during-first-phase-of-modernization-project/144129/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=NBC Chicago |date=29 April 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Blumberg |first1=Nick |title=Get Ready for Big Red Line Changes, CTA and City Warn |url=https://news.wttw.com/2020/01/28/get-ready-big-red-line-changes-cta-and-city-warn |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=WTTW |date=28 January 2020}}</ref> Due to a physically constrained construction area, the new viaduct was constructed out of [[Precast concrete|precast]] [[segmental bridge|segmental]] [[box girder bridge|box girders]] using a [[launching gantry]].<ref name="ENR 2021">{{cite news |last1=Yoders |first1=Jeff |title=Chicago Transit Untangles a Traffic Knot |url=https://www.enr.com/articles/51999-chicago-transit-untangles-a-traffic-knot |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Engineering News-Record |date=28 June 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Schultz |first1=Erin |last2=Buch |first2=Kevin |last3=Soule |first3=Ben |title=Precast Concrete Segmental Box Girders for the Red-Purple Modernization Program |url=https://aspirebridge.com/magazine/2023Spring/Project-PrecastConcreteSegmentalBoxGirdersForTheRed-PurpleModernizationProgram.pdf |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Aspire}}</ref>

Stage A began on May 16, 2021, with the closure of Lawrence and Berwyn stations and the opening of temporary station facilities at Argyle and Bryn Mawr stations. Trains were rerouted onto the two westernmost tracks to make way for the replacement of the two easternmost tracks.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wetli |first1=Patty |title=Pair of CTA Stations to Close Through 2024 as New Phase of Red-Purple Line Project Kicks Off |url=https://news.wttw.com/2021/05/13/pair-cta-stations-close-through-2024-new-phase-red-purple-line-project-kicks |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=WTTW |date=13 May 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Pathieu |first1=Diane |title=CTA announces reconstruction of 4 North Side Red Line stations |url=https://abc7chicago.com/post/cta-chicago-train-red-line-reconstruction/10530545/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=ABC7 Chicago |date=20 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Urbanize City">{{cite news |last1=Koziarz |first1=Jay |title=CTA readies massive Red Line overhaul in Uptown and Edgewater |url=https://chicago.urbanize.city/post/cta-readies-massive-red-line-overhaul-uptown-and-edgewater |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Urbanize Chicago |date=20 April 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

Stage A construction concluded on July 28, 2023, with the beginning of Stage B. Trains were rerouted onto two newly rebuilt tracks while construction began on the two westernmost tracks. Argyle station was relocated to Foster Avenue and Winona Street; Bryn Mawr station became only accessible to or from {{cta|95th}}-bound Red Line trains. Construction on permanent station facilities at Lawrence, Argyle, Berwyn, and Bryn Mawr stations began.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wanek-Libman |first1=Mischa |title=Final major stage of CTA's Red and Purple Modernization Phase One to begin July 28 |url=https://www.masstransitmag.com/rail/infrastructure/article/53066260/final-stage-of-ctas-red-and-purple-modernization-phase-one-to-begin-july-28 |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Mass Transit Magazine |date=17 July 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=CTA Sets Date for Red, Purple Modernization Phase One Project's Final Major Stage |url=https://www.metro-magazine.com/10202507/cta-sets-date-for-red-purple-modernization-phase-one-projects-final-major-stage |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=Metro Magazine |date=17 July 2023}}</ref>

These permanent facilities opened on July 20, 2025.<ref>{{multiref2
|{{cite news |last1=Masterson |first1=Matt |title=4 Reconstructed CTA Red Line Stops in Uptown, Edgewater Set to Open Next Month |url=https://news.wttw.com/2025/06/18/4-reconstructed-cta-red-line-stops-uptown-edgewater-set-open-next-month |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=WTTW |date=18 June 2025}}
|{{cite news |last1=McLawhorn |first1=Jennifer |title=Four CTA Red Line Stations Open July 20th Following Reconstruction |url=https://www.rtands.com/passenger/four-cta-red-line-stations-open-july-20th-following-reconstruction/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Railway Track and Structures |date=20 June 2025}}
|{{cite news |last1=Savedra |first1=Madison |title=New Far North Side Red Line Stations Open After Years Of Construction, Closures: 'We're So Excited' |url=https://blockclubchicago.org/2025/07/20/new-far-north-side-red-line-stations-open-after-years-of-construction-closures-were-so-excited/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |work=Block Club Chicago |date=20 July 2025}}
|{{cite news |title=CTA Red Line stations reopen after years-long renovation process |url=https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/renovated-cta-red-line-stations-reopen-for-first-time-in-4-years/3793602/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |work=NBC Chicago |date=20 July 2025}}
|{{cite news |last=Piekos |first=Christian |title=North Side CTA Red Line stations reopen after years of renovations |url=https://abc7chicago.com/post/north-side-cta-red-line-lawrence-argyle-berwyn-bryn-mawr-stations-reopen-years-chicago-renovations/17211054/ |access-date=20 July 2025 |work=ABC7 Chicago |date=20 July 2025 |language=en}}
}}</ref>

====Public space====
The replacement of embankment tracks opened up ten blocks of public space below the rail line. In 2024, during construction, the CTA held a series of public meetings on the new public space and its potential amenities.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ward |first1=Joe |title=Public Space Under Rebuilt Red Line Could Include Playgrounds, Walking Paths And Parking |url=https://blockclubchicago.org/2024/01/22/new-public-space-under-rebuilt-red-line-could-include-playgrounds-walking-paths-and-parking/ |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=Block Club Chicago |date=22 January 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=CTA to unveil designs for spaces under North Side Red Line tracks, schedules public meetings |url=https://abc7chicago.com/post/cta-to-unveil-designs-for-public-space-under-north-side-red-line-tracks-between-lawrence-and-ardmore-schedules-meetings/14751999/ |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=ABC7 Chicago |date=1 May 2024 |language=en}}</ref> The design for the space was finalized in February 2025 with the addition of a [[footpath]], parking spaces, and recreational amenities. Construction on the space is slated to occur from 2026 to 2027.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kugler |first1=Lukas |title=CTA unveils final design for blocks underneath new Red Line tracks |url=https://chicago.urbanize.city/post/cta-unveils-final-design-blocks-underneath-new-red-line-tracks |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=Urbanize Chicago |date=5 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Minné |first1=Hunter |last2=Dillinger |first2=Paige |title=CTA Releases Final Design Concepts for Spaces Under Renovated L Tracks |url=https://loyolaphoenix.com/2025/03/cta-releases-final-design-concepts-for-spaces-under-renovated-l-tracks/ |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=The Loyola Phoenix |date=12 March 2025}}</ref>
{{-}}

===Red-Purple Bypass===
[[File:Red-Purple Bypass overpass construction, January 2021 (cropped).jpg|thumb|alt=Construction on the Brown Line flyover ramp, viewed from Clark Street|Brown Line flyover ramp during its construction, January 2021]]

Before the project, Clark Junction was a level junction, which required northbound Brown Line trains to cross main line tracks at grade.<ref name="Clark Jct">{{cite web |last=Garfield |first=Graham |title=Clark Junction |url=https://www.chicago-l.org/operations/towers/clark.html |website=Chicago-L.org |access-date=27 July 2025}}</ref><ref name="MTM January 2022">{{cite news |last1=Wanek-Libman |first1=Mischa |title=CTA wraps up Red-Purple Bypass, begins North Belmont Red-Purple Reconstruction project |url=https://www.masstransitmag.com/rail/infrastructure/article/21254371/cta-wraps-up-red-purple-bypass-begins-north-belmont-red-purple-reconstruction-project |access-date=29 July 2025 |work=Mass Transit Magazine |date=25 January 2022 |language=en}}</ref>

The Red-Purple Bypass Project called for a {{convert|45|ft|m|adj=mid|-high}} Brown Line flyover ramp as well as a straighter alignment on the main line north of Belmont.<ref name="ENR 2021"/> The flyover was constructed out of steel [[plate girder]]s, while the new main line viaduct was largely constructed out of [[Precast concrete|precast]] [[Prestressed concrete|prestressed]] [[concrete girder bridge|concrete girders]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hereford |first1=Emily |last2=Depp |first2=David |last3=Johnson |first3=Amelia |title=Precast, Prestressed Concrete I-Beams for the Red-Purple Modernization Program |url=https://www.aspirebridge.com/magazine/2023Summer/Project-PrecastPrestressedConcreteIBeams-RedPurpleModernizationProgram.pdf |website=Aspire |access-date=16 July 2025}}</ref> With the exception of the straddle bent, which spans above the main line, the concrete [[Pier (bridge structure)|pier]]s for the flyover have decorative groove marks.<ref name="ENR 2021"/>

Construction began in 2019 with the installation of a flyover ramp.<ref name="ENR 2021"/> The flyover opened to Brown Line service on the early morning of November 19, 2021.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Freishtat |first1=Sarah |title=CTA’s new Brown Line flyover open near Belmont |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2021/11/19/ctas-new-brown-line-flyover-open-near-belmont/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=19 November 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Gallardo |first1=Michelle |title=CTA Red-Purple Bypass in service to ease congestion on Red, Purple, Brown Line trains |url=https://abc7chicago.com/post/cta-train-red-purple-bypass-project-flyover/11252998/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=ABC7 Chicago |date=19 November 2021 |language=en}}</ref> On March 3, 2022, inspectors reported concrete [[spalling]] on the flyover walls as a result of [[frost weathering]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Freishtat |first1=Sarah |title=Less than four months after opening, CTA's Brown Line flyover is undergoing repairs |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2022/03/03/less-than-four-months-after-opening-ctas-brown-line-flyover-is-undergoing-repairs/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=3 March 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Wittich |first1=Jake |title=Concrete Chunks Are Missing From New Brown Line Flyover, But CTA Says Contractor Knocked Them Off To Prevent Them From Falling |url=https://blockclubchicago.org/2022/03/03/concrete-chunks-are-missing-from-new-brown-line-flyover-but-cta-says-contractor-knocked-them-off-to-prevent-them-from-falling/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Block Club Chicago |date=3 March 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=McNicholas |first1=Tim |title=CTA Brown Line flyover just opened in November; why is concrete falling? |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/cta-brown-line-belmont-flyover-falling-concrete/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=CBS Chicago |date=3 March 2022}}</ref> Although the structural integrity of the flyover remained intact,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Horng |first1=Eric |title=Red-Purple bypass damaged mere months after opening, city says still perfectly safe to operate |url=https://abc7chicago.com/post/cta-red-line-purple-red-purple-bypass/11618736/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=ABC7 Chicago |date=4 March 2022 |language=en}}</ref> these damages were fully repaired in December 2022.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Wittich |first1=Jake |title=CTA's Brown Line Flyover Fixed By Contractor After Concrete Fell Off Shortly After Opening |url=https://blockclubchicago.org/2023/01/31/ctas-brown-line-flyover-fixed-by-contractor-after-concrete-fell-off-shortly-after-opening/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Block Club Chicago |date=1 February 2023}}</ref>

In August 2021, the [[Vautravers Building]] was moved westward to make way for straightening the main line north of Belmont.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Yan |first1=Jade |title=CTA begins moving historic Lakeview house 30 feet west as part of Brown Line flyover project |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/breaking/ct-cta-brown-line-historic-building-vautravers-20210802-zgxs7im3ovc3jprqkhlxkiulp4-story.html |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=Chicago Tribune |date=2 August 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Molina |first1=Nina |title=Historic Lake View building moving westward — literally — so Red Line tracks can be straightened |url=https://chicago.suntimes.com/2021/8/2/22606144/vautravers-building-lake-view-historic-cta-preservation-red-line-purple-move |access-date=27 July 2025 |work=Chicago Sun-Times |date=2 August 2021 |language=en}}</ref> Construction on the new alignment began in late 2021. The two westernmost tracks were first rebuilt, which reopened to service in December 2023. The two easternmost tracks were then closed for reconstruction until 2025.<ref>{{cite news |last1=McLawhorn |first1=Jennifer |title=CTA's RPM Phase One Project Begins Final Major Stage |url=https://www.rtands.com/passenger/ctas-rpm-phase-one-project-begins-final-major-stage/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Railway Track and Structures |date=6 December 2023}}</ref><ref name="MTM January 2022"/>
{{-}}

==Future phases==
The CTA is currently studying the rest of the phases surrounding the Evanston branch and the remaining segments of the North Side main line from Addison to Sheridan and from Thorndale to Howard. The RPM Next Phases Study was conducted from 2021 to 2024.<ref name="Loyola 2024">{{cite news |last1=Pentasuglio |first1=Julia |title=CTA Construction Plans Include Improving Loyola Red Line Stop |url=https://loyolaphoenix.com/2024/03/cta-construction-plans-include-improving-loyola-red-line-stop/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=The Loyola Phoenix |date=27 March 2024}}</ref> Several public meetings were held: two in March 2023,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mofus |first1=Olivia |title=CTA begins planning for Red and Purple Line renovations |url=https://dailynorthwestern.com/2023/04/09/city/cta-plans-red-and-purple-line-renovations-prioritizing-ada-accessibility-and-increased-capacity/ |access-date=3 October 2025 |work=The Daily Northwestern |date=10 April 2023}}</ref> one in November 2023, and one in February 2024.<ref name="Loyola 2024"/>

The project timeline is currently undetermined due to a lack of federal funding.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harrison |first1=Alex |title=CTA presents potential improvements for Purple Line |url=https://evanstonroundtable.com/2024/02/01/ready-to-edit-cta-presents-potential-improvements-in-purple-lines-future/ |access-date=16 July 2025 |work=Evanston RoundTable |date=2 February 2024}}</ref> In October 2025, at the start of the [[2025 United States federal government shutdown]], [[Office of Management and Budget]] director [[Russell Vought]] withheld a combined $2.1 billion for the Red Line Extension and the Red and Purple Modernization Project, citing reports of [[diversity, equity, and inclusion]] practices that he described as "unconstitutional".<ref name="Quig y411">{{cite web |last1=Quig |first1=A.D. |last2=Soglin |first2=Talia |last3=Yin |first3=Alice |date=October 3, 2025 |title=Mayor Brandon Johnson considering lawsuit as Trump withholds $2.1B from Chicago, including CTA Red Line Extension funds |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2025/10/03/trump-pauses-chicago-infrastructure-projects-shutdown/ |access-date=October 3, 2025 |website=Chicago Tribune}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web |last=Cherone |first=Heather |date=October 3, 2025 |title=Trump Pauses $2.1B for Chicago’s Red Line Extension and Other Infrastructure Projects, Citing ‘Race-Based Contracting’ |url=https://news.wttw.com/2025/10/03/trump-pauses-21b-chicago-s-red-line-extension-and-other-infrastructure-projects-citing |access-date=October 3, 2025 |website=WTTW News}}</ref>
